text.p: The following are the main stories from Tuesday morning's German newspapers:

- Metal employers and IG Metall union reach agreement to end their dispute over sick pay cuts for time being. They agree that for now the plans to cut pay to 80 percent for sick days will be shelved. Unions promise to halt work interruptions. Talks with continue on Thursday

- Kohl says the tax reform will take effect in January 1999. Although party leaders debate what groups can expect tax cuts and which may face new tax burdens, CDU party chairman Hintze says the principle will be: "lower taxes, simpler and fairer".

- Attacks on rail lines near Hannover and Berlin cripple train traffic. Several hundred trains were impacted by the attack, which police suspect may be linked to plans to transport nuclear waste to waste dump in Gorleben next month.
- Employers give up for now on plans to cut sick pay.
- German share prices reach record highs
- Finance Minister Theo Waigel says Bavarian Minister President Edmund Stoiber is all alone in his bid to introduce highway tolls in Germany.
- Metalworkers dispute defused. Daimler-Benz suspends plans to cut sick pay.
- German industrial leaders call for punctual start to European monetary union
- Allianz opens books on its holdings for the first time.
- Dispute over sick pay cuts defused
- Labour Minister Norbert Bluem rejects proposed tax on unemployment money
- Series of attacks on rail lines
